articles.title: NFL Makes Rule Change for In-Stadium Video Boards After Viral Photos of Patriots Gamesmanship
articles.summary: The NFL has reportedly informed teams that they must all use "the same All-22 angle or static image for both kicking teams" on video boards during field-goal and extra-point attempts, per ESPN's Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter.
articles.body:
The NFL has reportedly informed teams that they must all use "the same All-22 angle or static image for both kicking teams" on video boards during field-goal and extra-point attempts, per ESPN's Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter .

That rule change seemingly comes in response to a social media post from earlier in September that gave examples of the New England Patriots putting a reverse image of kicking attempts on their big board, leaving opposing kickers to see misaligned yellow goalposts on the screen behind the actual goalposts.

As he wrote, "When opposing kickers lined up at Gillette Stadium, the video board displayed a reverse view of the kick, placing a second, offset set of yellow uprights directly behind the real ones. In windy conditions, even the orange streamers on the video board appeared to point in the opposite direction from those atop the physical uprights, making the illusion even more disorienting."

Paganetti noted that in all of the games he reviewed, the Patriots never once used the reverse All-22 camera feed on the board for their own field goal or extra-point attempts.

Per ESPN's report, the Patriots were not breaking any rules at the time and other teams experimented with what they put on their video board as well.

As Reiss and Schefter wrote, "The NFL has long required all video and ribbon boards to display a static image—no flashing images, blinking effects, moving text/images etc.—or an All-22 view, such as the high-sideline or high-end-zone angle, during kicks."

Now, however, there will be no discrepancies between what is featured when each team is kicking.

articles.title: Stefon Diggs fined $14,926 for jumping on goal post after first Commanders touchdown; Jahmyr Gibbs fined $23,027 for head-first TD run
articles.summary: Diggs' penalty cost Washington a chance at a 2-point conversion, while Gibbs was not flagged for misuse of helmet during the game.
articles.body:
With Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season in the books, the fines are rolling in. The league announced the first round of them on Saturday, charging 20 individual players after a variety of offenses.

Among the big names on the list was Washington Commanders receiver Stefon Diggs , who was fined for unsportsmanlike conduct (illegal celebrations and vulgar acts) after a touchdown celebration.

After scoring his first touchdown as a Commander in the fourth quarter of Sunday's game against the Philadelphia Eagles , Diggs jumped onto the goal post and wrapped his legs around it.

Diggs was quickly flagged for the unsportsmanlike penalty, which denied Washington a chance to go for a 2-point conversion. The Commanders went on to lose 24-22 .

Afterward, Diggs admitted that he'd made a mistake.

"As soon as I wrapped my arms around it, I was like … 'Oh, I forgot.' It's not back in the day," Diggs said. "I've been playing for a long time. You used to [be able to] do that … I've got to be better."

Diggs' fine of $14,926 matches the league's punishment for a first offense on an unsportsmanlike conduct call. If Diggs were to commit another offense, he would be fined $20,897.

Also on the list was Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs , who was given the biggest fine of the week for improper use of helmet. The league charged Gibbs $23,027 for dropping his helmet into the chest of New Orleans Saints cornerback Quincy Riley on a touchdown run.

The play came on Gibbs' second rushing touchdown of the game, with the running back getting the score early in the third quarter. He was not flagged for the play.

In recent years, the league has cracked down on both use of helmet and unsportsmanlike conduct in games, charging hefty fines for both offenses. Though Diggs was the only player to be additionally punished for an illegal celebration, three others were fined for taunting.

As for Gibbs, the Lions RB was among three players to be fined for use of helmet violations. San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk received the second-biggest fine of the week ($20,033) after dropping his helmet while blocking .

Under NFL rules, a first offense for impermissible use of helmet or launching results in a $23,882 fine. It's unclear why Gibbs and Juszczyk were fined slightly less than that amount, though the NFL may have taken the plays on case-by-case basis.

articles.summary: Green Bay Packers linebacker Lukas Van Ness did not receive a fine for his involvement in the hit that resulted in Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray suffering a concussion in Week 1, per Josh Alper of Pro Football Talk.
articles.body:
Green Bay Packers linebacker Lukas Van Ness did not receive a fine for his involvement in the hit that resulted in Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray suffering a concussion in Week 1, per Josh Alper of Pro Football Talk.

Van Ness and Packers safety Javon Bullard hit Murray as he was scrambling outside the pocket in the first quarter of Minnesota's 39-22 win over Green Bay, as the signal-caller was subsequently ruled out for the remainder of the game.

Bullard received an unnecessary roughness penalty at the time.

Van Ness was fined $17,911 by the NFL for a separate play in which his hand made contact with the head of Vikings backup quarterback Carson Wentz in the third quarter of the contest, per ESPN's Rob Demovsky .

The Packers jumped out to a 22-10 lead following Murray's exit in the first half, although the Vikings racked up 29 unanswered points to emerge victorious.

Minnesota also outscored Green Bay 22-0 in the fourth quarter.

Van Ness finished with four tackles and one sack, while Bullard recorded one tackle.

Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell didn't place blame on either player for Murray's injury after the game.

"It would be one thing if there was a headfirst slide and a clear declaration [of giving himself up]," O'Connell explained, per ESPN's Kevin Seifert . "But I don't put any fault on anybody there."

Van Ness hasn't developed a reputation for racking up fines throughout his career, as he was only fined twice across 43 total games heading into the 2026 season (via Spotrac ).

As for Murray, he was ruled out of Minnesota's Week 2 clash with the Chicago Bears due to the concussion.

ESPN's Dan Graziano reported Friday that Murray has continued to progress through concussion protocol and "did more in practice Thursday than Wednesday" despite ultimately being unable to suit up.

Wentz will start for the Vikings on Sunday.

articles.title: NFL implements stricter rules for images displayed on stadium video boards during field goals and extra points after Patriots' ploy is uncovered
articles.summary: A former NFL analytics coach discovered that the Patriots displayed goalposts on their video board, creating visual distortion for kickers.
articles.body:
NFL teams are now restricted on what can be shown on stadium video boards during field-goal and extra-point attempts, per a directive from the league issued prior to the beginning of the 2026-27 season.

Teams must display a static image or a standard wide-angle, All-22 view on the jumbo-sized screens behind the end zone as kicks are taking place, the NFL mandated in a memo sent to each organization, according to ESPN .

NFL rules have always mandated that moving, flashing, blinking images and texts could not be shown on video boards during field-goal and extra-point tries. To prevent undue distractions or unfair advantages to home teams, only static images could be displayed on video boards.

However, those rules have been modified to more closely restrict even images that aren't moving on the screen, ESPN's Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter reported .

The stricter regulations were implemented in response to a social-media post by a former NFL analytics coach that pointed out images displayed by the New England Patriots on the Gillette Stadium video board that presented an optical illusion to opposing place-kickers.

Ryan Paganetti — who worked for the Philadelphia Eagles , Jacksonville Jaguars and Las Vegas Raiders — posted several screen shots from 10 years' worth of Patriots game broadcasts that showed an All-22 view of the field incorporating the goalposts behind the end zone. The image was offset from the actual uprights in the stadium, creating potential visual confusion as to where the goalposts were located.

The former coach added in his post that the wide-field view including goalposts was never shown on the video board when Patriots kickers were attempting field goals or extra points in 52 examples he reviewed.

Under the previous guidelines regarding video-board images, the Patriots did not break any rules. The image shown was static. No moving image or text was on the screen. Other teams experimented with what could be displayed on the board as well, according to the NFL.

But now, under the stricter regulations, NFL teams are only allowed to show a standardized All-22 angle (one that presumably doesn't include goalposts) or other static image. And the same image has to be displayed for both teams attempting field goals and extra points in order to prevent any sort of potential competitive advantage.

The NFL warned in its memo that any teams violating the stricter rule would face discipline from the league.

COLLEGE STATION - Kentucky stunned No. 9 Texas A&M with 21 consecutive points during the third quarter Saturday to pull off a 31-21 upset victory.

The Wildcats gained 196 total yards in the third quarter while the Aggies netted only 20 yards and failed to convert a fourth down deep in their territory, shifting a 7-7 halftime score at a 28-7 deficit for A&M.

Wildcats quarterback Kenny Minchey threw for 252 yards and two touchdowns and former Texas running back CJ Baxter had two touchdowns.

The Aggies offense entered the game without wide receiver Ashton Bethel-Roman and running back Jamarion Morrow due to injuries.

Then wideout and returner Terry Bussey , who entered the game second in receiving yards, had to be carted off after suffering an injury on the opening kickoff.

But their absences weren't the main issue for the A&M offense. Instead it was execution and finishing drives.

A 4th-and-1 rush at the Kentucky 11 from Rueben Owens II got stuffed for no gain. A bad Marcel Reed interception terminated another promising first-half drive. A couple of Reed incompletions then cut short the Aggies' first half's final possession with the score tied at 7.

But luckily for Texas A&M , Kentucky entered halftime ruing missed chances of its own: a missed 39-yard field goal from Adam Zouagui and a drop from Kenny Darby on what would have been a touchdown pass if completed.

Darby got redemption at the start of the second half on a 42-yard touchdown pass. Then Baxter reached the end zone to cap the following two drives.

Meanwhile, Texas A&M couldn't get anything going on offense. The momentum was slipping so far away that Mike Elko elected to go for it on 4th-and-2 at his own 33 down 21-7. But Reed's pass while rolling out to Carsyn Baker hit the ground. A good pass would have moved the chains.

Texas A&M went for it on fourth down again in the fourth quarter, this time a desperate 4th-and-13 from its own 22 down 31-14. Reed scrambled through the middle of the field for a 40-yard gain.

But then just a few plays later he threw the ball well wide of wideout TK Norman and right into the hands of Jordan Castell for an interception.

Reed finished 26-of-49 for 236 passing yards plus 80 rushing yards.
